extracted.intended_audience: general readers, fans, and researchers looking for an encyclopedic summary of the TV sitcom 'Workaholics'.
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article summarizing a television sitcom: its premise/synopsis, cast, production history, episode/season data, home media releases, and critical and audience reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series metadata (genre, network, release, seasons, episodes, running time)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article records core metadata: Genre: Sitcom; Country of origin: United States; Original language: English; No. of seasons: 7; No. of episodes: 86; Running time: 21 min. (25 min. series finale); Original release: April 6, 2011 – March 15, 2017; Network: Comedy Central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factual attributes are used to classify and document a TV series. They serve as baseline descriptors for readers and researchers (e.g., identifying the show as an American adult sitcom on Comedy Central with seven seasons and 86 episodes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Synopsis / premise clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The synopsis summarizes the premise: three college dropouts who are housemates, friends, and co-workers at a telemarketing company in Rancho Cucamonga, California, continuing college-era behavior (drinking, partying, pulling pranks) and interacting in settings like their house, their drug dealer, and their shared cubicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An effective encyclopedic synopsis concisely conveys main characters, setting, recurring situations, and the show's central comedic themes (friendship-family dynamic, juvenile antics, workplace conflict).

rubrics_metrics.name: Production and creation history
rubrics_metrics.description: Details about creators, showrunners, directors, production companies, origin story: created and largely written by Blake Anderson, Adam DeVine, Anders Holm, Kyle Newacheck; frequent director/co-creator Kyle Newacheck; showrunner Kevin Etten; ordered by Comedy Central after an executive saw YouTube videos from Mail Order Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documenting creators, production companies, directorial and showrunning roles, and the origin (e.g., discovery via online videos) explains how the series was developed and greenlit—information relevant to understanding creative control and production context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode/season broadcast chronology and renewal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Chronology of seasons and episode counts (Season 1: 10 eps; Season 2: 10 eps; Season 3: 20 eps split across broadcasts; Seasons 4–7 counts and air dates). The article notes renewals tied to popularity (e.g., Comedy Central ordered additional seasons because of the show's popularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broadcast schedules, episode splits, and explicit links between popularity/viewership and network renewal decisions are presented as evidence of commercial success and programming strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative audience metrics (ratings & viewership)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nielsen ratings and viewership figures are cited: Season 2 premiere first to attain over two million audience; highest rating 2.16 (Season 2, episode 'Teenage Mutant Ninja Roommates'); Season 2 averaged about 1.64 million viewers per episode; Season 3 premiere achieved a 2.11 in Nielsen ratings; later episodes show drop-offs with final three episodes achieving ~1.23–1.24 million.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nielsen ratings and average viewers are used as quantitative measures of popularity and commercial performance; trends (peaks and declines) are used to contextualize the show's audience trajectory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical reception (qualitative critical descriptors and sources)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical evaluations from outlets are summarized: The A.V. Club's Kevin McFarland called it 'a more adult version of Ed, Edd n Eddy'; Metacritic described Season 1 as 'mixed or average reviews'; Boston Globe (Matthew Gilbert) called the first season 'witty, irreverent, and joyously juvenile'; Dave Wiegand said 'The material works more often than not because the guys are completely shameless.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical adjectives and quoted judgments illustrate how reviewers evaluate tone, comedic style, and effectiveness. Citing named outlets and reviewers provides authority and reflects the range of critical opinion (positive to mixed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Home media release details and special features
rubrics_metrics.description: Home releases are enumerated with formats, release dates, included episodes, and special features (e.g., Season 1 DVD/Blu-ray Oct 11, 2011: cast interviews, deleted scenes, Digital Originals, alternate takes, audio commentary; The Complete Series: June 20, 2017, includes all 86 episodes on 15 discs and all special features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Home media specifications (format, disc counts, special features) document how the series is packaged post-broadcast and can indicate value offered to collectors/fans.
